name: Focus Visible
explanation: Any interface that can be operated by keyboard must have some visible way to see which element currently has keyboard focus. This is usually the browser's default focus outline. Many sites remove it with CSS, like `outline: none`, for aesthetic reasons, without adding a visible replacement. This criterion doesn't specify exactly what the focus indicator has to look like. It just has to exist and actually be visible when a keyboard user tabs through the page, so the browser default is a perfectly valid way to satisfy it.
whoItAffects: Keyboard-only users have no other way to know which element on the page is currently active. That element is what would respond to Enter, Space, or arrow keys. Without a visible focus indicator, they're navigating blind, unable to tell where they are on the page. Sighted keyboard users rely on this same visual cue too. This group includes people with motor disabilities who can't use a mouse, and people who simply prefer keyboard navigation for speed.
howToTest: Tab through the entire page using only the keyboard. Watch closely as focus moves from one element to the next. At every stop, is there a clearly visible indicator, such as an outline, border, or background change, showing which element currently has focus? Suppose focus ever becomes invisible on an interactive element, such as a link, button, or form field. That's a failure of this criterion.

check.question: A site's CSS includes the rule `*:focus { outline: none; }` applied globally, with no alternative focus styling added anywhere else in the stylesheet. Does this pass SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible?
choices: Yes, because removing the default outline is a common design choice
No, because keyboard focus has been made invisible with no visible replacement provided
Yes, because mouse users are unaffected by this change
It depends only on whether the site uses a dark or light color theme
